"Our Father, who art in heaven, holy be thy name. Thy Kingdom come, thy will be done, at some distant point in the future in accordance with our prophecy charts..."

Actually, no. That's not how it goes. 

Let me show you how Baptists interpreted this clause in the Lord's Prayer long before Darby invented the heresy of Dispensationalism. 

From Keach's Catechism (1693): 

"In the second petition, which is, 'Thy kingdom come,' we pray that Satan’s kingdom may be destroyed, and that the kingdom of grace may be advanced, ourselves and others brought into it and kept in it, and that the kingdom of glory may be hastened."

And...

"In the third petition, which is, 'Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven,' we pray that God by his grace would make us able and willing to know, obey, and submit to his will in all things, as the angels do in heaven."

What you might not know is that Phil Johnson's Dispensationalism teaches that the Lord's Prayer, cited here, wasn't even for Christians in the modern age. Did you know that? Probably not: they hide that part of their beliefs because it's so obscene. 

Darby said of the Lord's Prayer, “This chapter does not go into what we may call proper church privileges" (“Notes on the Gospel of Luke,” in The Collected Writings of J. N. Darby, vol. 25, Expository No. 4, p. 115). 

"It's for the Jews only." Lol. No, it isn't. 

Darby does the same as Johnson. He discourages Christians from doing anything useful, saying in that clause that if we are active in doing good, "we shall be in danger of being tired with running, which is always wrong. We should be in the spirit of waiting pilgrims, not weary ones."

Don't get tired. Don't run the race. Sit. Wait. Do nothing. 

Scofield says the same, "Used as a form, the Lord’s prayer is, dispensationally, upon legal, not church ground; it is not a prayer in the name of Christ…” 

QUESTION: So why is Phil Johnson even citing the Lord's Prayer if it's not even for us Christians? ANSWER: So he can refute its use to accomplish things in the world. And that's pretty sick. 

What @DefiantBaptist shows you here in this clip is not Christian theology. It's the fever dream of a schismatic Irish heretic in 1827 who thought up his doctrines while in his sickbed for a week. And what he created is a Judaizing hodgepodge of charts and graphs that sodomize the Scriptures to make it come together and appear like a coherent theology. And does so poorly.

In 1971, John MacArthur attended the infamous Jerusalem Prophecy Conference with his "mentor and discipler," Charles Feinberg (the last name is no coincidence), funded and sponsored by the State of Israel. 

That's where MacArthur says he became most convinced of Dispensationalism 2.0, a version different from Darby's, which rewrote the prophecy chart timelines to make 1948 a prophetic fulfillment ex post facto. It was also far, far more militantly Zionist than the original Scofield editions. 

That group of men, 1,500 in total, were inducted into the first graduating class of Israel's first brought-and-paid American ministers whose job was to push this bastardized theology throughout the American church. 

And the product? 

The product today is a group of men, like Phil Johnson, standing here at MacArthur's old pulpit, urging American Christians to not lift a finger to stop our civilizational decline. 

Every attempt to do God's will on Earth is characterized as disobedience. 

Every effort to make a difference is seen as a lack of faith. 

Every desire to become salt (preserving our culture) is projected as an impediment to being light (sharing the gospel). 

The full counsel of God's Word has been limited to the gospel. Being useful has been replaced with calls for deeper prayers, longer sermons, and more frequent church attendance. 

Preaching, replaced with lectures. Action, replaced with endless commentary. Zeal, replaced with godless apathy. The Great Commission, replaced by Jack Chick tracts and Grace to You cassettes.

And it's all done blasphemously in Jesus' name, while viciously attacking those who, in Jesus' name, coalesce to inform the world that Christ is their King. 

Grace Community Church has lost its pastor, and is now dwindling. And that's odd, considering the crowd will get the same sermons, written by all the same people as before. Only the deliverer is different. 

You see, these men already have a kingdom come. It serves no one but them, but it's still a brick-and-mortar kingdom with millions of dollars each year, funded by people who think the message of "don't lift a finger" is useful. 

They have no reason to want God's "Kingdom Come" because they have their own kingdom to worry about, and anyone who insists Christians should *do something* challenges theirs. And they meet them with the highest level of rage and hostility, all for the sin of believing that Christians have a job to do that doesn't involve giving more tithe, singing louder, and buying the next book. 

Grace is never extended to them. They get endlessly lectured about the sin of doing something, and the transgression of not sitting idly to show your commitment to their teaching. 

The Millerites who awaited Christ's return in the Great Disappointment had to sell their farms and not plant crops that year in order to prove their commitment to the prophecy chart. But MacArthur's kingdom must similarly prove its faith by doing nothing. At least the Millerites' demands had an expiration date. It's no wonder both systems are Restorationist cults. 

Part of God's own Kingdom Come is destroying theirs. And may the Lord Jesus destroy it in the brightness of His coming. 

Meanwhile, move forward. Ignore them. They'll all be dead soon. And we have work to do. 

Onward.
